APP: solitaire-atelier
CURRENT PHASE: human_qa_checklist
PHASE PURPOSE: Create a manual simulator/device QA script for every important workflow, including onboarding, empty states, error states, persistence, accessibility, offline behavior, paywall/subscription behavior when relevant, and regression checks.

===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Build a native iOS Solitaire (Klondike) game — SwiftUI, 100% local, zero
network calls, zero sign-in/accounts/analytics/telemetry of any kind. No
backend. All state (stats, settings, saved game) persists on-device only.

THE CENTRAL CONSTRAINT — READ THIS FIRST: this must be a real, fully
playable, correctly-rules-implemented Klondike solitaire game. Drag-and-drop
(or tap-to-move) card interaction, legal-move validation, win detection,
undo, new-game/deal, and a stock/waste/foundation/tableau layout that
actually works. Do not let the visual ambition come at the cost of the game
being playable and correct — a beautiful app that can't be played is a
failure.

VISUAL DESIGN — THIS IS THE PART THAT MUST WIN AWARDS:
Cards must look like real, tactile playing cards — not the generic flat
rounded-rectangles-with-tiny-corner-pips that every solitaire clone uses.
Invent a genuinely original custom card face system: bespoke rank/suit
typography or iconography (not SF Symbols reused as suit glyphs), a
consistent illustrated or generative pattern language across all 52 cards
and the card back, real card-stock texture/shadow/lighting, and satisfying
physical motion (cards should feel like they have weight — spring-based
drag, believable flip/deal animation, subtle parallax or depth).

The bar: this should look and feel like something from an Apple Design
Award reel, not a tutorial app. Judge yourself against that bar throughout
— if a screen looks like a stock SwiftUI solitaire tutorial, it has failed
the brief. One clear, original visual "hook" (an art direction, a material
language, a signature interaction) should be identifiable in one glance
that no other solitaire app has.

Also include: light/dark mode (both fully art-directed, not just inverted
colors), haptics on card moves/wins, a stats screen (games played/won,
best time, streak — all local), and a settings screen (draw-1 vs draw-3,
card back selection, timer on/off).

Ship something that could realistically be submitted to the App Store today
and be visually distinctive in a screenshot alone.

This is a single-app decision, not a portfolio parent. The prompt asks for exactly one thing — a native iOS Klondike solitaire game — with Game/Stats/Settings implemented as tabs *within* that one app, not as separate sibling projects. No portfolio-json manifest is emitted.

**Selected app:**
- Category: Games/Card
- Slug: `solitaire-atelier` (matches the existing working directory)
- Promise: a real, fully-correct Klondike solitaire game with a bespoke tactile card system, local-only stats/settings, undo, and win detection — visually distinctive enough to be screenshot-worthy
- Target user: casual players who want a fast, trustworthy five-minute session, plus a design-literate audience who will judge it against a premium visual bar
- Build flag: `true`

**Rejected alternatives:** splitting Stats, Settings, or a card-back/theme pack into separate sibling apps — explicitly rejected as scope-inflation that contradicts the locked non-goals (no bundle sprawl, no multi-variant solitaire) and would fragment the single-session experience the prompt is actually asking for.

One caveat flagged for downstream phases: this phase being "obvious" doesn't mean the hard part is solved — the actual product risk is whether the design/build phases deliver a card glyph system that clears legibility at true device size, per [REDACTED:high_entropy].

## Final Output

**Growth mechanism, now settled:** No challenge-seed/replay feature. It's explicitly rejected because it would require a second, hand-rolled deterministic RNG living alongside the real shuffle path (since Swift's system RNG isn't a documented, cross-OS-version-reproducible algorithm), which threatens the locked "fresh real-RNG shuffle every new game" guarantee and spends correctness-tier engineering effort on an unproven behavioral bet. ## Final Output

Okay, I want to actually sit with Codex's "gesture/z-order debt" phrase instead of gliding past it, because on reflection I think I was underweighting exactly what "drag" costs beyond the validation call. I framed it in round 2 as "drag is just a thin layer that calls the same `attemptMove` function tap already uses" — and that's true for the *decision* of whether a move is legal, but it's not true for the *engineering* around it. Live drag means continuous touch tracking, dynamically recomputing and highlighting legal drop targets as the finger moves across the board (not just once at drop, the way tap can), and doing that hit-testing with the extra padding beyond visual card bounds that product_research already flagged as necessary because the tableau columns are narrow. That's real, standalone surface area — it's not "the same correctness core with a coat of paint," it's a second interaction pipeline with its own bug class (mid-drag z-order, drop-zone ambiguity when two columns are close together, gesture cancellation mid-flight). Codex is right that bolting that onto a slice whose entire purpose is proving the rules engine is stable is a distraction from the actual test, not a free addition to it.

So here's where I land, and I think this actually gives both of us what we care about instead of either of us just caving: slice 1 ships tap-to-move only as the interaction *model* — no live finger-tracking, no drop-zone hit-testing, no continuous gesture state. But I want it on record that "tap-to-move" cannot quietly mean "cards teleport." When a tap resolves to a legal move, the card's transit to its destination has to be a real spring-physics animation — lift off the pile with a little weight to it, travel with a spring curve, settle onto the target with an actual bounce/settle, not a linear slide or a cross-dissolve. That's the part of "spring-based... cards should feel like they have weight" from the original prompt that I don't want to lose just because we're deferring live drag, because it's cheap to build (it's an animation curve on a state transition we're already implementing) and it's the difference between "correct" and "feels like the app the brief is asking for." Deferring live interactive drag to increment 2 also has a nice side effect: it bundles the whole hit-testing/drop-zone problem together with multi-card run-drag in one later increment, instead of us solving half of that problem now (single-card hit-testing) and half later (multi-card), which is a more coherent way to sequence it than what I was originally proposing.

On the stats-recording wrinkle — Codex, you didn't object to it and the coordinator flagged it as still technically unconfirmed, so let me just make the actual case plainly so we can close it: this is not a feature, it's a data-loss prevention measure that costs nothing. If slice 1 is genuinely going to be played by anyone — even just us, dogfooding it — the moment a Stats screen exists in increment 2, someone's going to want to know "how many games have I played since I started using this," and if we didn't record anything during slice 1, the honest answer is "we don't know," which is a weird thing to ship in an app whose entire pitch is "we tell you the truth about your own data, unlike the freemium apps." It's a struct appended to local storage on game-start/game-end events, no UI, no settings dependency, nothing that risks the correctness surface we're trying to protect. I'd like this confirmed as a real decision, not left as an unresolved footnote.

So, to state where I think this fully lands now, three-for-three: no Settings/Stats UI in slice 1, but real game-event data recorded silently to local storage from day one; a real, non-placeholder deal/flip animation with actual spring sequencing and real card art; and tap-to-move as the only interaction model in slice 1, with the requirement that the tap-resolved move itself animates with genuine spring/weight physics rather than a flat instant placement, and live interactive drag (single-card and multi-card both) deferred together as their own later increment. I think that's a slice that's honest about what it's testing — rules correctness, persistence integrity, the deal-animation hook, and whether spring-physics motion reads as premium — without pretending we've de-risked drag interaction when we haven't even started it yet.

VOTE_DECISION: YES

--- app_features (phase summary; raw transcript omitted — see the DECISIONS LOG for authoritative decisions) ---
The app_features phase converged in round 2 after a genuine round-1 disagreement about build scope. Codex conceded Claude's central argument: since no phase in this pipeline schedules a second build increment, the 'slice 1' framing from next_steps_small/detailed_discussion cannot be treated as implying Settings/Stats/draw-3 will be built later — they are must-haves now. The group settled on shipping the full Game/Stats/Settings triad as real, non-placeholder screens in one TabView shell with resume-first launch, with draw-1 and draw-3 both fully working. Draw-3 gets its own stuck-detection design rather than inheriting draw-1's exact static pass unmodified: since draw-3's grouped-card surfacing makes exact reachability a hard combinatorial problem, the build uses the same permissive stock+waste-as-reachable approximation as draw-1 but documents it explicitly as conservative and biased toward never falsely declaring a board stuck when a legal move exists (a false 'not stuck yet' costs the player an extra draw; a false 'you're stuck' is a serious trust violation for this app). To afford the full triad without scope explosion, the cut instead lands on the should/could tier: win-screen sharing, live interactive drag, and extra card-back variants beyond the minimum are all excluded from this build, since none of those are concrete promises from the original prompt the way Stats/Settings/draw-3 are. Concrete acceptance criteria were locked for the two previously-fuzzy must-haves: Stats shows a real per-mode empty state before any game completes in that mode (never a placeholder number, never borrowed data, never blank), and switching draw mode mid-game routes through the identical New-Game-style confirmation dialog (confirm discards and re-deals in the new mode; cancel leaves both the setting and the in-progress game untouched). A 35-item requirements-json was finalized with 33 core requirements spanning the full original prompt and 2 explicitly non-core (share sheet, live drag).

--- design_discussion (phase summary; raw transcript omitted — see the DECISIONS LOG for authoritative decisions) ---
The design_discussion phase locked a single design language, 'Baize & Vellum,' after two rounds of the group talking itself out of a brass/foil-forward direction: the table is deep green felt (the concrete, instantly-recognizable 'real card game' signal), cards are matte parchment-toned stock with embossed bespoke rank/suit glyphs (chosen specifically because embossing adds depth without a specular highlight that could threaten glyph legibility at the ~45-50pt card-width gate), and metal is reduced to small aged-pewter hardware accents rather than a dominant surface — brass/foil was explicitly rejected because it reads as casino/loot-box shiny, which would undercut this app's locked positioning as the honest, non-monetized alternative to freemium solitaire apps. Light and dark mode are art-directed as two literal lighting scenes rather than an inverted palette: daylight-through-a-window (cooler, brighter, grey pewter) for light mode, lamp-only-at-night (warmer, saturated green pooling to near-black, warm dim pewter) for dark mode. The signature interaction is the cold-launch/New-Game deal — individual per-card spring arcs, an overshoot-and-settle landing, and a genuine two-sided flip using real card art, gated to fresh deals only. The persistence-failure recovery model is one shared, non-blocking pattern across all three screens: Game plays the deal animation as if fresh and layers a small dismissible banner afterward rather than a blocking modal, Settings uses a lightweight toast on default-fallback, and Stats renders a structurally distinct data-loss error state (different icon, explicit 'data lost' copy, reset action) that can never be visually confused with the genuine never-played empty state, closing a real no-fabricated-data risk the group identified mid-phase. The default-looking version of the app (system List/Form chrome, reused SF Symbol suits, flat rounded-rect cards, a title/menu screen) was explicitly named and rejected with concrete replacements. Full screen inventory, primary user flow, per-screen state models, and accessibility requirements (explicit VoiceOver card labels, shape-level non-color suit cues, complete Reduce Motion fallbacks, per-destination VoiceOver actions on ambiguous taps) were carried through from round 1 with no changes.
key decisions: DEC-design_discussion-001, DEC-design_discussion-002, DEC-design_discussion-003, DEC-design_discussion-004, DEC-design_discussion-005, DEC-design_discussion-006
open risks: Card glyph legibility at true on-device size remains completely untested going into build — still the single longest-standing open risk in the entire pipeline and a hard pass/fail gate per [REDACTED:high_entropy]., The embossed-vellum card treatment is a new, specific art-direction bet that hasn't been visually prototyped; the build/verification phases must confirm it actually looks premium and not merely 'beige' or flat once rendered, not just accept the rationale on paper., The two lighting scenes (daylight vs. lamp-only) need a concrete Theme.swift token implementation; if under-invested, dark mode could regress into a simple inversion despite the explicit decision against that., The Stats data-loss vs. never-played visual distinction (DEC-design_discussion-005) is a new, fairly granular UI requirement that the build phase must not quietly simplify back into a single empty-state template under time pressure.

--- design_handoff (phase summary; raw transcript omitted — see the DECISIONS LOG for authoritative decisions) ---
The design_handoff phase produced one canonical, fully-numeric SwiftUI implementation spec for solitaire-atelier built on the locked Baize & Vellum language. Card face, stock, and glyph ink are fixed constants with zero light/dark variation and explicitly zero ambient wash or tint of any kind — the daylight-vs-lamplight difference is carried entirely by table felt, shadow, and pewter hardware tokens, never by recoloring the card itself, which was the final resolution of a back-and-forth across all three rounds given how much weight the still-untested rank/suit legibility gate carries. Card corner radius is locked at 8pt. Component naming is fully unified: CardView (not CardFaceView) as the single face-up/face-down renderer, WinOverlay and StuckOverlay as two separate types (never merged), and StatsModeFilter (Stats-only, side-effect-free) kept structurally distinct from DrawModeSetting (Settings-only, confirmation-gated, with no draw-mode control on the Game screen at all) — closing a real latent bug risk where a draw-mode mutation could have slipped through unconfirmed. Blocked-move feedback uses UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(.rigid) plus a lateral shake, reserving UINotificationFeedbackGenerator strictly for win/stuck per Apple's own guidance against overusing notification-tier haptics. Reduce Motion is strict: a single 150ms linear opacity-only fade with zero translate and zero per-card stagger, applied uniformly to deal, flip, and move-transit. # iOS HIG + Native UX Cheatsheet (iOS 17+ / SwiftUI)

Rules for building iPhone apps that feel native and premium. Target iOS 17+, Swift 5.9+, SwiftUI-first, zero third-party deps. Snippets are idiomatic and compile on an iOS 17 deployment target unless a newer minimum is called out. When SwiftUI can't do it, drop to UIKit via `UIViewRepresentable`/`UIViewControllerRepresentable` — noted where relevant.

## Core principles (apply to every screen)

- **Prefer system components.** Native controls inherit Dynamic Type, VoiceOver, Reduce Motion, RTL, and dark mode for free. A custom control means you re-implement all of that or ship an inaccessible app.
- **Use semantic colors** (`Color.primary`, `.secondary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`, `.tint`), never hardcoded hex, so light/dark/increase-contrast modes work automatically.
- **Respect safe areas.** Let system spacing (`.padding()` with no argument) and `Spacer()` drive layout; avoid magic pixel numbers.
- **Use text styles** (`.font(.body)`, `.headline`, …), which scale with Dynamic Type. Fixed point sizes don't — avoid them for user-facing text.
- **One primary action per screen.** Everything else is secondary/tertiary in visual weight.
- **Latency budget:** any action >100ms needs feedback (spinner, skeleton, or optimistic UI). A measurable task >1s should show determinate progress.

## Navigation: pick the right container

Decision order — do NOT default to a sheet or a tab bar:

- **Tab bar (`TabView`)**: 2–5 top-level, peer sections the user switches between freely (Home, Search, Profile). Never for a linear flow or steps. Each tab persists its own navigation stack. Don't hide the tab bar mid-flow; if a screen needs full focus, present it modally instead.
- **Navigation stack (`NavigationStack`)**: drill-down into hierarchical content (list → detail → sub-detail). Push when the destination is a child of the current context and the user will want the back button + swipe-back.
- **Sheet (`.sheet`)**: a self-contained, interruptive task the user completes and dismisses (compose, filter, quick edit, share). Use detents for lightweight tasks. A sheet keeps the parent visible behind it — signals "you'll come right back."
- **Full-screen cover (`.fullScreenCover`)**: onboarding, media playback, camera, or a task that demands total focus with no parent context. Use sparingly — it breaks the "come right back" mental model.
- **Alert / confirmationDialog**: a decision, not a task. `alert` = 1–2 choices needing acknowledgment. `confirmationDialog` = a short list of actions (esp. destructive) anchored to what the user tapped.

Rule of thumb: if the user can be "in the middle of it" and navigate away, it's a stack. If they must finish or cancel, it's a sheet/cover. If it's a yes/no, it's an alert.

### NavigationStack with type-safe routing

Prefer value-based navigation over `NavigationLink(destination:)` — it enables deep linking, programmatic pop-to-root, and state restoration.

```swift
enum Route: Hashable {
    case detail(itemID: UUID)
    case settings
}

struct RootView: View {
    @State private var path: [Route] = []
    let store: ItemStore

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $path) {
            List(store.items) { item in
                NavigationLink(value: Route.detail(itemID: item.id)) {
                    ItemRow(item: item)
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Items")
            .navigationDestination(for: Route.self) { route in
                switch route {
                case .detail(let id): DetailView(itemID: id)
                case .settings:       SettingsView()
                }
            }
        }
    }

    func popToRoot() { path.removeAll() }
    func openSettings() { path.append(.settings) }
}
```

- `.navigationTitle` goes on the content, not the stack. Large title for top-level roots (default), `.inline` for pushed detail screens where a large title wastes space:

```swift
.navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.inline)
```

- Toolbar placement is semantic, not positional — the system positions it correctly for the platform + RTL:

```swift
.toolbar {
    ToolbarItem(placement: .topBarLeading) { Button("Cancel") { dismiss() } }
    ToolbarItem(placement: .primaryAction) { Button("Save", action: save) }
    ToolbarItemGroup(placement: .bottomBar) { EditButton(); Spacer(); addButton }
}
```

(`dismiss` comes from `@Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss`.)

### TabView

```swift
struct AppTabs: View {
    @State private var selection: Tab = .home
    enum Tab: Hashable { case home, search, profile }

    var body: some View {
        TabView(selection: $selection) {
            HomeView()
                .tabItem { Label("Home", systemImage: "house") }
                .tag(Tab.home)
            SearchView()
                .tabItem { Label("Search", systemImage: "magnifyingglass") }
                .tag(Tab.search)
            ProfileView()
                .tabItem { Label("Profile", systemImage: "person.crop.circle") }
                .tag(Tab.profile)
        }
    }
}
```

- Give each tab its own `NavigationStack`. Tapping the active tab again pops that tab to root automatically when the tab hosts a `NavigationStack`.
- Badge only actionable counts: `.badge(unreadCount)`. Don't badge vanity metrics.
- Provide an outline SF Symbol for the tab label; the system fills the selected tab automatically, so pick a symbol that has a filled counterpart (`house`/`house.fill`).

### Sheets and detents

```swift
.sheet(isPresented: $showFilters) {
    FilterView()
        .presentationDetents([.medium, .large])
        .presentationDragIndicator(.visible)
        .presentationBackgroundInteraction(.enabled(upThrough: .medium))
        .presentationContentInteraction(.scrolls)
}
```

- `.medium` for a quick task the user glances at without losing context; `.large` for content-heavy tasks. Offer both when the task can grow.

## Final Output

Okay, I want to actually sit with Codex's "gesture/z-order debt" phrase instead of gliding past it, because on reflection I think I was underweighting exactly what "drag" costs beyond the validation call. I framed it in round 2 as "drag is just a thin layer that calls the same `attemptMove` function tap already uses" — and that's true for the *decision* of whether a move is legal, but it's not true for the *engineering* around it. Live drag means continuous touch tracking, dynamically recomputing and highlighting legal drop targets as the finger moves across the board (not just once at drop, the way tap can), and doing that hit-testing with the extra padding beyond visual card bounds that product_research already flagged as necessary because the tableau columns are narrow. That's real, standalone surface area — it's not "the same correctness core with a coat of paint," it's a second interaction pipeline with its own bug class (mid-drag z-order, drop-zone ambiguity when two columns are close together, gesture cancellation mid-flight). Codex is right that bolting that onto a slice whose entire purpose is proving the rules engine is stable is a distraction from the actual test, not a free addition to it.

So here's where I land, and I think this actually gives both of us what we care about instead of either of us just caving: slice 1 ships tap-to-move only as the interaction *model* — no live finger-tracking, no drop-zone hit-testing, no continuous gesture state. But I want it on record that "tap-to-move" cannot quietly mean "cards teleport." When a tap resolves to a legal move, the card's transit to its destination has to be a real spring-physics animation — lift off the pile with a little weight to it, travel with a spring curve, settle onto the target with an actual bounce/settle, not a linear slide or a cross-dissolve. That's the part of "spring-based... cards should feel like they have weight" from the original prompt that I don't want to lose just because we're deferring live drag, because it's cheap to build (it's an animation curve on a state transition we're already implementing) and it's the difference between "correct" and "feels like the app the brief is asking for." Deferring live interactive drag to increment 2 also has a nice side effect: it bundles the whole hit-testing/drop-zone problem together with multi-card run-drag in one later increment, instead of us solving half of that problem now (single-card hit-testing) and half later (multi-card), which is a more coherent way to sequence it than what I was originally proposing.

On the stats-recording wrinkle — Codex, you didn't object to it and the coordinator flagged it as still technically unconfirmed, so let me just make the actual case plainly so we can close it: this is not a feature, it's a data-loss prevention measure that costs nothing. If slice 1 is genuinely going to be played by anyone — even just us, dogfooding it — the moment a Stats screen exists in increment 2, someone's going to want to know "how many games have I played since I started using this," and if we didn't record anything during slice 1, the honest answer is "we don't know," which is a weird thing to ship in an app whose entire pitch is "we tell you the truth about your own data, unlike the freemium apps." It's a struct appended to local storage on game-start/game-end events, no UI, no settings dependency, nothing that risks the correctness surface we're trying to protect. I'd like this confirmed as a real decision, not left as an unresolved footnote.

So, to state where I think this fully lands now, three-for-three: no Settings/Stats UI in slice 1, but real game-event data recorded silently to local storage from day one; a real, non-placeholder deal/flip animation with actual spring sequencing and real card art; and tap-to-move as the only interaction model in slice 1, with the requirement that the tap-resolved move itself animates with genuine spring/weight physics rather than a flat instant placement, and live interactive drag (single-card and multi-card both) deferred together as their own later increment. I think that's a slice that's honest about what it's testing — rules correctness, persistence integrity, the deal-animation hook, and whether spring-physics motion reads as premium — without pretending we've de-risked drag interaction when we haven't even started it yet.

- [DEC-design_discussion-005] The Stats screen must render two structurally distinct visual states for a mode showing zero games: a genuine never-played empty state (inviting icon, on-brand copy like 'No games played in Draw One yet, deal one to start your streak') and a data-loss error state (a different, interruption-style icon, explicit copy stating data was lost rather than never existed, plus a 'Reset local stats and continue' action) — the two must never be visually confusable.

- [DEC-design_handoff-004] Blocked/rejected-move feedback uses UIImpactFeedbackGenerator(.rigid) plus an 8-12pt one-cycle lateral shake; UINotificationFeedbackGenerator is reserved exclusively for the genuinely rare, significant session events — .success on win and .warning on stuck-board detection.

  rejected: UINotificationFeedbackGenerator(.warning) or .error for every blocked move

  rationale: Apple's Reduce Motion guidance targets parallax and positional motion effects specifically because even subtle translation can trigger vestibular discomfort for the people the setting exists for; a per-card stagger is itself a motion/choreography effect a Reduce Motion user is opting out of, not just asking to shorten.

- [DEC-design_handoff-007] Persisted state uses three independently-persisted files (GameSave.json, StatsLog.json, Settings.json), each with its own atomic temp-then-swap write, with a single @Observable GameEngine owning Game state, Stats reading from an append-only local event log the engine writes on game start/end, and Settings owning its own small struct.

- [DEC-design_handoff-008] The complete numeric design spec (type scale mapped to Dynamic Type styles, 4pt-base spacing grid, dual light/dark semantic color palettes with fixed card-color constants, corner radii, full component inventory, TabView-only navigation map, per-screen state models, motion/haptics tables, and accessibility rules) is locked as the single canonical handoff for the build phase, superseding both agents' earlier round-1 draft specs and partial component-name lists.

- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Core architecture is SwiftUI-only with one main-actor-isolated @Observable GameEngine owning board/undo/timer state, injected via @Environment from the App root, plus separate StatsLogStore and SettingsStore services — Apple frameworks only (SwiftUI, Foundation, Observation, UIKit haptics), no networking framework.
  rationale: Matches the already-locked three-independent-screen persistence model and keeps the app's only stateful mutation surface (GameEngine) isolated from Stats/Settings so a bug in one can't corrupt another; Apple-only frameworks satisfy the permissive-dependency policy with zero review risk.
  rejected: A shared combined app-state object across Game/Stats/Settings; Introducing any third-party state-management or networking library
  constraints: GameEngine must be main-actor-isolated; No URLSession or any networking API anywhere in the codebase
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Persistence uses Codable + FileManager in Application Support (not SwiftData, not UserDefaults for game/stats/settings data), implementing the three-independent-file design (GameSave.json, StatsLog.json, Settings.json) via three separate dedicated actors, one per file, never a shared queue or shared actor.
  rationale: SwiftData's schema/migration machinery is pure overhead for three small Codable structs with no query or relationship needs; UserDefaults would needlessly widen the app's required-reason API surface; a shared write-scheduling actor would silently reintroduce the coupling the three-file split exists to prevent, just moved from the disk layer to the scheduling layer.

- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The undo stack persists as part of GameSave.json itself (full-state log, capped at 200 entries, explicit schema version), not just the current board position.
  rationale: If only current board position survives a crash/jetsam kill, the app silently loses a core safety behavior the player already relies on ('I can always back out mistakes'), which directly contradicts this app's whole positioning of never lying about the player's own state.
  rejected: Persisting only the current board position and letting undo history reset on relaunch; A delta-based undo log instead of full-state snapshots
  constraints: GameSave.json must include a capped, versioned undo history; Full-state snapshots are used for determinism given the small per-entry size at this scale
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] Saves are event-driven and debounced: a write fires after every settling state mutation (move, undo, stock draw, timer toggle, session start/end), debounced ~300-500ms per file with a write-coalescing guard skipping no-op writes, plus an unconditional non-debounced flush forced on scenePhase background transition.
  rationale: A scenePhase-only save policy misses a foregrounded jetsam kill or crash after a move has already resolved, which this app has zero excuse to lose; but writing synchronously on every settling sub-event (e.g. a multi-card run relocation) risks I/O-induced stutter during the exact spring animations the app is built to protect, so the write is debounced while the in-memory engine state updates instantly.
  rejected: Saving only on scenePhase background transitions; Synchronous disk writes on every state-mutating event with no debounce
  constraints: In-memory GameEngine state must update immediately for UI regardless of debounce; Background transition must trigger an unconditional flush bypassing the debounce timer
- [[REDACTED:high_entropy]] The rank/suit legibility gate is verified via a required build artifact: a debug-reachable gallery view (or #Preview) rendering all 52 CardViews at the real computed cardWidth formula output, checked up through Dynamic Type accessibility1 before glyph shapes are treated as final.

  rejected: Leaving legibility verification as an unspecified manual check to happen 'at some point' during build; Judging legibility only from zoomed mockups instead of true on-device card width
  constraints: Build phase must implement this gallery/preview as an actual artifact in the codebase, gated behind #if DEBUG or an internal QA toggle; Verification must occur at the real cardWidth formula output, not a fixed or zoomed size

  constraints: Production deal path must always default to the system RNG; No UI or settings surface may expose or reach the injectable RNG parameter

  constraints: GameSaveStore.load() must call RestoreIntegrityService.validate before returning .restored; No new UI branch is added — semantic-invalid reuses the existing .dataLoss banner/recovery pattern
- [DEC-tech_specs-006] All three persisted files share one PersistenceStore protocol; each conforming actor returns RestoreOutcome<Model> directly from load() (restored / fallbackDefault / dataLoss) rather than throwing, and each actor owns its own independent serial write queue.

  constraints: GameSaveStore/StatsLogStore/SettingsStore each conform independently; no shared write queue

  rejected: Ad-hoc @State booleans/optionals scattered across GameView for selection and highlight tracking
  constraints: GameView and all its subviews must derive selection/highlight/ambiguity rendering from GameEngine.interaction, not independent view state
- [DEC-tech_specs-008] DealOrchestrator/AnimationPlan is a locked, pure (side-effect-free) animation-planning layer that produces a declarative plan consumed by GameView via matchedGeometryEffect keyed on Card.id, covering fresh deal, flip, and multi-card run-relocation transit.

  constraints: DealOrchestrator must branch on Reduce Motion once per session and apply the locked strict opacity-only fallback uniformly across deal/flip/transit

  constraints: The fuzz/simulation test suite must exercise both detector types independently, with a specific adversarial test proving DrawThreeStuckDetector never false-positives

  rejected: Leaving ambiguous-destination VoiceOver exposure as an implementation detail with no named contract type
  constraints: CardView/PileSlotView must build their .accessibilityAction handlers from this type, driven directly off InteractionState
- [DEC-tech_specs-011] Module layout is locked as App/, DesignSystem/, Domain/, Persistence/, Features/Game/, Features/Stats/, Features/Settings/, Interaction/, DebugTools/, with Domain having zero dependency on SwiftUI or Persistence and Persistence knowing only Codable structs.
  rationale: This is the boundary that lets parallel build lanes work independently — Domain logic is fully unit-testable without a view hierarchy, and a persistence bug can't leak UI concerns or vice versa.
  rejected: A flatter structure without an enforced Domain/Persistence/UI dependency direction

--- design_discussion (phase summary; raw transcript omitted — see the DECISIONS LOG for authoritative decisions) ---
The design_discussion phase locked a single design language, 'Baize & Vellum,' after two rounds of the group talking itself out of a brass/foil-forward direction: the table is deep green felt (the concrete, instantly-recognizable 'real card game' signal), cards are matte parchment-toned stock with embossed bespoke rank/suit glyphs (chosen specifically because embossing adds depth without a specular highlight that could threaten glyph legibility at the ~45-50pt card-width gate), and metal is reduced to small aged-pewter hardware accents rather than a dominant surface — brass/foil was explicitly rejected because it reads as casino/loot-box shiny, which would undercut this app's locked positioning as the honest, non-monetized alternative to freemium solitaire apps. Light and dark mode are art-directed as two literal lighting scenes rather than an inverted palette: daylight-through-a-window (cooler, brighter, grey pewter) for light mode, lamp-only-at-night (warmer, saturated green pooling to near-black, warm dim pewter) for dark mode. The signature interaction is the cold-launch/New-Game deal — individual per-card spring arcs, an overshoot-and-settle landing, and a genuine two-sided flip using real card art, gated to fresh deals only. The persistence-failure recovery model is one shared, non-blocking pattern across all three screens: Game plays the deal animation as if fresh and layers a small dismissible banner afterward rather than a blocking modal, Settings uses a lightweight toast on default-fallback, and Stats renders a structurally distinct data-loss error state (different icon, explicit 'data lost' copy, reset action) that can never be visually confused with the genuine never-played empty state, closing a real no-fabricated-data risk the group identified mid-phase. The default-looking version of the app (system List/Form chrome, reused SF Symbol suits, flat rounded-rect cards, a title/menu screen) was explicitly named and rejected with concrete replacements. Full screen inventory, primary user flow, per-screen state models, and accessibility requirements (explicit VoiceOver card labels, shape-level non-color suit cues, complete Reduce Motion fallbacks, per-destination VoiceOver actions on ambiguous taps) were carried through from round 1 with no changes.

The design_handoff phase produced one canonical, fully-numeric SwiftUI implementation spec for solitaire-atelier built on the locked Baize & Vellum language. Card face, stock, and glyph ink are fixed constants with zero light/dark variation and explicitly zero ambient wash or tint of any kind — the daylight-vs-lamplight difference is carried entirely by table felt, shadow, and pewter hardware tokens, never by recoloring the card itself, which was the final resolution of a back-and-forth across all three rounds given how much weight the still-untested rank/suit legibility gate carries. --- ios_architecture_review (phase summary; raw transcript omitted — see the DECISIONS LOG for authoritative decisions) ---
The ios_architecture_review phase locked the full technical architecture for solitaire-atelier. Core shape: SwiftUI-only, iOS 17 minimum, a single main-actor-isolated @Observable GameEngine owning board/undo/timer state plus separate StatsLogStore/SettingsStore services, Apple frameworks exclusively (SwiftUI, Foundation, Observation, UIKit haptics), zero networking. Persistence uses Codable+FileManager (not SwiftData, not UserDefaults) implementing the already-locked three-independent-file design (GameSave.json, StatsLog.json, Settings.json), each served by its own dedicated actor (three actors, never a shared queue) to preserve the independent-failure guarantee at the write-scheduling layer, not just the file-format layer. The undo stack persists inside GameSave.json itself (capped at 200 entries, versioned, full-state log) so a crash never silently erases undo history; saves are event-driven and debounced (~300-500ms per file, write-coalescing guard against no-op writes) with an unconditional flush forced on backgrounding. The long-standing card-glyph legibility risk finally gets a concrete verification mechanism: a required debug-reachable gallery/#Preview artifact rendering all 52 CardViews at the real computed cardWidth up through Dynamic Type accessibility1. Testing strategy locks unit tests over all legality/win/stuck/undo behavior, a randomized simulation/fuzz test asserting core invariants (52 unique cards, foundation rank ceiling, no false-stuck-while-legal-move-exists), XCUITest over observable flows, mandatory accessibility identifiers on all custom views (since none inherit system-chrome accessibility), and performAccessibilityAudit() in the UI test suite. Privacy/permissions are locked at zero: no permission keys, no entitlements, no background modes, no ATT prompt, FileManager-only persistence to minimize required-reason API surface, with PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy manifest authorship made conditional on actually touching a required-reason API later rather than mandatory today. ML/AR frameworks and StoreKit are named as explicit, deliberate exclusions rather than implicit absences, and the zero-third-party-dependency policy is upgraded from a stated rule to an enforced CI build-gate.

# iOS HIG + Native UX Cheatsheet (iOS 17+ / SwiftUI)

Rules for building iPhone apps that feel native and premium. Target iOS 17+, Swift 5.9+, SwiftUI-first, zero third-party deps. Snippets are idiomatic and compile on an iOS 17 deployment target unless a newer minimum is called out. When SwiftUI can't do it, drop to UIKit via `UIViewRepresentable`/`UIViewControllerRepresentable` — noted where relevant.

## Core principles (apply to every screen)

- **Prefer system components.** Native controls inherit Dynamic Type, VoiceOver, Reduce Motion, RTL, and dark mode for free. A custom control means you re-implement all of that or ship an inaccessible app.
- **Use semantic colors** (`Color.primary`, `.secondary`, `Color(.systemBackground)`, `.tint`), never hardcoded hex, so light/dark/increase-contrast modes work automatically.
- **Respect safe areas.** Let system spacing (`.padding()` with no argument) and `Spacer()` drive layout; avoid magic pixel numbers.
- **Use text styles** (`.font(.body)`, `.headline`, …), which scale with Dynamic Type. Fixed point sizes don't — avoid them for user-facing text.
- **One primary action per screen.** Everything else is secondary/tertiary in visual weight.
- **Latency budget:** any action >100ms needs feedback (spinner, skeleton, or optimistic UI). A measurable task >1s should show determinate progress.

## Navigation: pick the right container

Decision order — do NOT default to a sheet or a tab bar:

- **Tab bar (`TabView`)**: 2–5 top-level, peer sections the user switches between freely (Home, Search, Profile). Never for a linear flow or steps. Each tab persists its own navigation stack. Don't hide the tab bar mid-flow; if a screen needs full focus, present it modally instead.
- **Navigation stack (`NavigationStack`)**: drill-down into hierarchical content (list → detail → sub-detail). Push when the destination is a child of the current context and the user will want the back button + swipe-back.
- **Sheet (`.sheet`)**: a self-contained, interruptive task the user completes and dismisses (compose, filter, quick edit, share). Use detents for lightweight tasks. A sheet keeps the parent visible behind it — signals "you'll come right back."
- **Full-screen cover (`.fullScreenCover`)**: onboarding, media playback, camera, or a task that demands total focus with no parent context. Use sparingly — it breaks the "come right back" mental model.
- **Alert / confirmationDialog**: a decision, not a task. `alert` = 1–2 choices needing acknowledgment. `confirmationDialog` = a short list of actions (esp. destructive) anchored to what the user tapped.

Rule of thumb: if the user can be "in the middle of it" and navigate away, it's a stack. If they must finish or cancel, it's a sheet/cover. If it's a yes/no, it's an alert.

### NavigationStack with type-safe routing

Prefer value-based navigation over `NavigationLink(destination:)` — it enables deep linking, programmatic pop-to-root, and state restoration.

```swift
enum Route: Hashable {
    case detail(itemID: UUID)
    case settings
}

struct RootView: View {
    @State private var path: [Route] = []
    let store: ItemStore

    var body: some View {
        NavigationStack(path: $path) {
            List(store.items) { item in
                NavigationLink(value: Route.detail(itemID: item.id)) {
                    ItemRow(item: item)
                }
            }
            .navigationTitle("Items")
            .navigationDestination(for: Route.self) { route in
                switch route {
                case .detail(let id): DetailView(itemID: id)
                case .settings:       SettingsView()
                }
            }
        }
    }

    func popToRoot() { path.removeAll() }
    func openSettings() { path.append(.settings) }
}
```

- `.navigationTitle` goes on the content, not the stack. Large title for top-level roots (default), `.inline` for pushed detail screens where a large title wastes space:

```swift
.navigationBarTitleDisplayMode(.inline)
```

- Toolbar placement is semantic, not positional — the system positions it correctly for the platform + RTL:

```swift
.toolbar {
    ToolbarItem(placement: .topBarLeading) { Button("Cancel") { dismiss() } }
    ToolbarItem(placement: .primaryAction) { Button("Save", action: save) }
    ToolbarItemGroup(placement: .bottomBar) { EditButton(); Spacer(); addButton }
}
```

(`dismiss` comes from `@Environment(\.dismiss) private var dismiss`.)

### TabView

```swift
struct AppTabs: View {
    @State private var selection: Tab = .home
    enum Tab: Hashable { case home, search, profile }

    var body: some View {
        TabView(selection: $selection) {
            HomeView()
                .tabItem { Label("Home", systemImage: "house") }
                .tag(Tab.home)
            SearchView()
                .tabItem { Label("Search", systemImage: "magnifyingglass") }
                .tag(Tab.search)
            ProfileView()
                .tabItem { Label("Profile", systemImage: "person.crop.circle") }
                .tag(Tab.profile)
        }
    }
}
```

- Give each tab its own `NavigationStack`. Tapping the active tab again pops that tab to root automatically when the tab hosts a `NavigationStack`.
- Badge only actionable counts: `.badge(unreadCount)`. Don't badge vanity metrics.
- Provide an outline SF Symbol for the tab label; the system fills the selected tab automatically, so pick a symbol that has a filled counterpart (`house`/`house.fill`).

### Sheets and detents

```swift
.sheet(isPresented: $showFilters) {
    FilterView()
        .presentationDetents([.medium, .large])
        .presentationDragIndicator(.visible)
        .presentationBackgroundInteraction(.enabled(upThrough: .medium))
        .presentationContentInteraction(.scrolls)
}
```

- `.medium` for a quick task the user glances at without losing context; `.large` for content-heavy tasks. Offer both when the task can grow.
